title: Design Slack
prompt:
Design a team chat product organised into workspaces. Each workspace has public and private channels, direct messages, threads, file sharing and full-text message search. Members must only ever see data they are allowed to see.

Assume **30 million daily active users** across several hundred thousand workspaces, about **100 messages per user per day**, channels with up to **100,000 members**, and workspaces with up to 500,000 users.
clarify: Are channels public, private or both, and can guests or external organisations join?
What are the largest channel and workspace sizes?
How fresh must search results be, and is search across all channels or only joined ones?
Do we need unread counts, mentions, threads, edits and deletes with audit/retention rules?
Is data isolation per customer a hard requirement (enterprise, regional residency)?

reference.requirements:
**Functional**
- Workspaces, public/private channels, DMs, threads, mentions, reactions
- Real-time delivery, unread badges, edits and deletes
- Search messages and files, limited to what the caller may read
- Admin controls and retention policies

**Non-functional**
- Delivery < 1 s to online members
- Hard tenant isolation: no cross-workspace leakage, even through bugs or search
- Heavy tenants must not starve small ones
- Searchable within a few seconds of sending
reference.estimation:
- Messages: 30M × 100 = 3B/day ≈ **35k writes/s** avg
- Storage: 3B × ~300 B = **900 GB/day** ≈ 330 TB/year before replication; the search index adds roughly the same again
- Large-channel fanout: a message in a 100k-member channel, if pushed to everyone, is 100k deliveries, but only the ~10% online and connected matter
- Read-state: one cursor per (user, channel) pair; 30M users × ~30 channels ≈ **900M cursors** × ~24 B ≈ 22 GB, easily cached
reference.api:
```
POST /v1/channels/{id}/messages {client_id, text, thread_ts?}   → {msg_id}
GET  /v1/channels/{id}/messages?before=&limit=
POST /v1/channels/{id}/read     {last_read_msg_id}
GET  /v1/search?q=&workspace=&cursor=
WS   /rt   (events: message, reaction, channel_updated, presence)
```
- The token is **scoped to one workspace**; every call checks `workspace_id` and channel membership.
- Sending goes over HTTP POST, receiving over WebSocket, which keeps the write path load-balanceable.
reference.data:
- Every table carries `workspace_id`, and it is in every index.
- `channels(workspace_id, channel_id, type, name)`; `channel_members(channel_id, user_id)` **and** `user_channels(user_id, channel_id)` (denormalised both ways: fanout needs the first, "my sidebar" needs the second).
- `messages(channel_id, msg_id, user_id, text, thread_ts, deleted_at)` sharded by `channel_id`, clustered by `msg_id` (Snowflake: time + shard + sequence).
- `read_cursor(user_id, channel_id, last_read_msg_id)`.
- Files in object storage with access checked via a signed, short-lived URL.
reference.design:
```
client ─ws▶ gateway ─┐                     ┌─▶ search indexer ─▶ search cluster
client ─http▶ API ─▶ message service ─▶ msg store
                        │  └▶ pub/sub ─▶ gateways hosting members ─▶ clients
                        └▶ notification svc ─▶ push for offline members
search: client ─▶ search API ─▶ index shard(workspace) + membership filter
```
- **Message path:** write to the store (durable), then publish an event; gateways with subscribed members forward it; an indexer and the notification service consume the same event.
- Gateways only hold connections; they ask the channel service which channels a user has.
reference.deepdives:
- **Channel fanout by size.** For DMs and small channels, publish per recipient. For large channels, publish once to the channel and let each gateway that hosts a member subscribe and fan out locally; only online members are pushed. Offline members get no write at all: when they return, they compare their `read_cursor` to the channel's latest id to compute unread state. Trade-off: unread counts are derived at read time (or by lazy counters) instead of maintained per member.
- **Search with permissions.** Index per workspace (or route by `workspace_id`), and filter by the channels the caller can read. Resolve that set at query time from membership (cached) rather than baking ACLs into documents, since membership changes constantly. Private-channel messages must stay hidden after a user leaves, so a delete or removal needs a cheap filter path, not reindexing. Index lag of seconds is acceptable.
- **Tenancy and hotspots.** `workspace_id` in every key and token scope is the first line of defence, with per-workspace rate limits against noisy neighbours. Shard messages by `channel_id`, not workspace, so one giant tenant spreads across shards; keep metadata and search routed by workspace. Big enterprises can get a dedicated cell.
- **Deletes and retention.** Soft-delete first, then a retention job removes the text, index entries and files.
reference.wrapup:
- The split is: messages sharded by channel, membership and read-state kept as small cursors, search as an eventually consistent derived index.
- Trade-offs: push vs pull per channel size, query-time ACL filtering vs index-time, workspace vs channel sharding.
- Next: threads, presence, edits and compliance export.

rubric.text: Estimates write rate, storage growth and notes the search index adds substantially to it
Puts workspace_id in every table, key and index, and scopes auth tokens to a workspace
Models channel membership both ways (channel to users, user to channels) and explains why
Shards messages by channel and uses time-sortable ids (Snowflake) for ordering and pagination
Delivers in real time over WebSocket gateways via pub/sub, persisting before publishing
Switches fanout strategy by channel size: per-recipient for small, per-channel subscription for large
Derives unread state from per-user read cursors instead of writing to every member
Builds search as an asynchronous derived index, per workspace, with eventual freshness
Enforces permissions in search by filtering on channels the caller can read at query time
Addresses noisy neighbours: per-workspace rate limits, cells/dedicated shards for large tenants
Covers deletes, edits and retention propagating to the index and files
